headline: Napatree Breachway Loaded with Albies, First Green Crab Tog Show at Sakonnet
subhead: Bunker and silversides are stacking the rips from Watch Hill to Second Beach, and the tog bite is starting to wake up on the deeper ledges.
body_markdown:
Walk the wrack line at Napatree this week and you'll see it before you cast a thing — silversides pinned against the sand in nervous sheets, peanut bunker balled up tight off the point, and sand eels working the edge of the reef at Watch Hill on the last of the ebb. That's the whole story right there. The bait has finally packed into the corners where the current squeezes it, and everything that eats moved in behind it.

The Harvest Moon tides did exactly what big tides do this time of year — they pushed more water, moved more bait, and pulled fish tight to structure where they could pin it. We flagged this pattern last week, saying the blitz intensity would build as more bait got flushed south, and that's exactly what's playing out along the breachways. Napatree, Watch Hill Reef, and the mouth of the Sakonnet are all holding consistent albie and bonito action, with fish pushing through on the moving tide and vanishing on the slack. Water's still holding in the upper 60s off the open beaches, which is keeping the false albacore invasion rolling harder and later into the season than most years.

Albies are eating small — 2 1/2-inch Albie Snax in bone or pink-white, and 3-inch Deadly Dick jigs worked with a fast, erratic retrieve through the rip at Napatree Point on the incoming. Same story at the Weekapaug breachway and the east side of Watch Hill Reef, where the current lines up cleanest on the first two hours of the flood. Bonito are mixed in but scattered — smaller profile baits, size 2 Deceivers in olive-over-white, have been drawing more looks than the bigger albie candy. Sakonnet Point is holding its own push of albies right off the rocks below the light, best worked on the outgoing when bait gets pulled out of the harbor and funneled past the breakwater.

Striped bass are stacking up behind the bunker schools now, and that pattern should only get stronger as the week goes. Second Beach and the beaches around Sachuest are seeing bass working peanut bunker pods just outside the wash, especially at first light and again on the last hour of daylight. Snag-and-drop with a bunker on a treble under a popping cork has been the most consistent producer, though guys throwing bunker-profile swimbaits — 6-inch paddletails in bunker or white — off the rocks at Jamestown's east passage breakwaters have been connecting too. Bluefish are riding along with every one of these blitzes, chopping up bait on the surface and giving away the whole show with the diving birds. Nothing monstrous size-wise yet, mostly 3- to 6-pounders, but they'll hit anything moving fast.

Tog are just starting to wake up on the deeper ledges, and this is the piece of the report worth paying attention to if you're tired of chasing breaking fish. Green crabs are producing on the rockpiles off Beavertail in Jamestown and along the base of the Newport Bridge pilings, fished tight to the structure on slack water — the tog haven't moved off the summer rocks yet, but the cooler nights are nudging them deeper, and the bite window is widening each week. Sakonnet Point's boulder fields, right where the current breaks around the point, are holding fish too, best worked right at the top or bottom of the tide when the drift eases up and you can hold bottom without dragging.

Scup and porgy remain the bread-and-butter bite for anyone who wants a full cooler without the run-and-gun. Structure around the Jamestown Bridge, the Newport Harbor moorings, and the rockier stretches off Second Beach are all holding fish on squid strips and green crab pieces, size 4 or 6 hooks on a simple high-low rig. Nothing glamorous, but it's about as sure a thing as this zone offers right now.

Looking ahead, expect the albie push to keep building through the week as long as the warm-water pattern holds offshore — the breachways from Napatree to Sakonnet should keep producing on the tide changes, with the better window typically the two hours around the turn when bait gets squeezed through the gut. Bass numbers behind the bunker should keep climbing as the moon tides continue moving bigger volumes of bait along the open beaches. The one thing worth watching is any real cold front pushing through toward the end of the month — that's usually what starts tipping water temps hard enough to accelerate the bass south and put the tog bite into full swing on the ledges. Until then, work the moving water, keep an eye on the birds working the breachways, and don't sleep on the rocks just because the blitzes are grabbing the headlines.
